items.followUp: Differentiate between competitive and non-competitive inhibitors.

rubric.why: Identifies the effect of inhibitors on enzyme activity.
rubric.description: Inhibitors decrease enzyme activity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that inhibitors slow or reduce enzyme activity.

rubric.why: Identifies the effect of activators on enzyme activity.
rubric.description: Activators increase enzyme activity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that activators speed up or increase enzyme activity.

modelAnswer: Inhibitors decrease or stop the activity of enzymes.
Activators increase the activity of enzymes.

items.followUp: Arrange the taxonomic categories from species to kingdom and give one example.

rubric.why: Tests the correct sequence of taxonomic categories.
rubric.description: Lists the categories in order from lower to higher.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the complete correct sequence; award 1 mark if one category is missing or misplaced.

rubric.why: Shows understanding of the place of species in classification.
rubric.description: Identifies species as the basic or smallest taxonomic unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying species as the basic unit of classification.

rubric.why: Explains how organisms are grouped into taxonomic categories.
rubric.description: Explains that each higher category groups related organisms from the category below it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation of grouping related organisms.

modelAnswer: Taxonomic hierarchy is the arrangement of organisms into successive categories, from the smallest to the largest.
The categories in ascending order are species, genus, family, order, class, phylum and kingdom.
Species is the basic unit of classification and consists of similar organisms that can interbreed.
A genus contains related species; each successively higher category groups related members of the category below it.

items.followUp: Define photosynthesis and describe the role of chlorophyll in the light reactions.

rubric.why: Assesses the definition of photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Defines photosynthesis as the process by which green plants use light energy to make food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning green plants, light energy and food or chemical energy.

rubric.why: Assesses the location of the light reactions.
rubric.description: States that light reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes of the grana in chloroplasts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the grana or thylakoid membranes as the site.

rubric.why: Assesses the role of photosynthetic pigments in the light reactions.
rubric.description: Explains that chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chlorophyll absorbs or traps light.

rubric.why: Assesses the breakdown of water during the light reactions.
rubric.description: States that light energy splits water molecules (photolysis).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the light-driven splitting of water.

rubric.why: Assesses the products of the light reactions.
rubric.description: Names oxygen as a released product and/or ATP and NADPH as energy-rich products.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly naming the products formed or released.

modelAnswer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy to make food from carbon dioxide and water.
Light reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes of the grana in chloroplasts.
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
This energy splits water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen; this process is called photolysis.
Oxygen is released, while ATP and NADPH are formed for use in the next stage of photosynthesis.

items.followUp: Define transpiration and explain how humidity and wind affect its rate.

rubric.why: Assesses the definition of transpiration.
rubric.description: Defines transpiration as the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through stomata.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water vapour loss from aerial parts or through stomata.

rubric.why: Assesses the effect of temperature on transpiration.
rubric.description: Explains that higher temperature increases transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly linking higher temperature to a higher rate.

rubric.why: Assesses the effect of atmospheric humidity.
rubric.description: Explains that high humidity decreases transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that humid air reduces the water-vapour gradient and transpiration.

rubric.why: Assesses the effect of wind or air movement.
rubric.description: Explains that wind generally increases transpiration by removing moist air around the leaf.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing the effect of wind and its cause.

rubric.why: Assesses another factor that affects transpiration.
rubric.description: Explains one additional factor, such as light, leaf area or number of stomata.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct effect of one additional internal or external factor.

modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of leaves.
High temperature increases evaporation and usually increases the rate of transpiration.
High humidity decreases transpiration because the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and air is reduced.
Wind generally increases transpiration by carrying away moist air from around the leaf.
Light usually increases transpiration because stomata open; a larger leaf area or more stomata can also increase the rate.

items.followUp: State two characteristics of a scientific theory.

rubric.why: Tests whether the student knows that a hypothesis must be testable.
rubric.description: A good hypothesis must be testable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it can be tested by investigation or experiment.

rubric.why: Tests whether the student knows what a hypothesis should be based on.
rubric.description: A good hypothesis should be based on observations or existing evidence and knowledge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying an appropriate evidential basis.

modelAnswer: A good hypothesis must be testable.
It should be based on observations or existing evidence and knowledge.

items.followUp: Give two differences between plant cell walls and animal cells.

rubric.why: Tests the difference in thickness of the two walls.
rubric.description: The primary wall is thin, while the secondary wall is thick.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct thickness comparison.

rubric.why: Tests the difference in formation or composition.
rubric.description: The primary wall forms while the cell grows; the secondary wall is deposited inside it after growth and may contain lignin.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison of formation or composition.

modelAnswer: The primary wall is thin and is formed while the cell is growing; the secondary wall is thicker and is deposited inside the primary wall after growth has stopped.
The primary wall is mainly made of cellulose, while the secondary wall may contain additional substances such as lignin.

items.followUp: Where are ribosomes found, and what is their function?

rubric.why: Assesses the membrane status of ribosomes.
rubric.description: Ribosomes are non-membranous structures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ribosomes lack a surrounding membrane.

rubric.why: Assesses the basic structure of a ribosome.
rubric.description: Each ribosome consists of a large and a small subunit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both subunits or stating that there are two subunits.

modelAnswer: Ribosomes are small, non-membranous structures made of ribosomal RNA and proteins.
Each ribosome consists of a large subunit and a small subunit.

items.followUp: Write the scientific names of wheat and the house mouse.

rubric.why: Assesses the scientific name of onion.
rubric.description: Gives the scientific name of onion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correctly written binomial name.

rubric.why: Assesses the scientific name of the house crow.
rubric.description: Gives the scientific name of the house crow.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correctly written binomial name.

modelAnswer: Onion: Allium cepa
House crow: Corvus splendens
